title: Complex images lose recognizable features under lossy compression

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complex images lose recognizable features under lossy compression

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Under lossy compression by keeping only some basic forms (as in JPEG-like schemes), the relevant features of both simple and completely random images remain recognizable at high compression, whereas images normally considered complex need much lower compression, and reordering the basic forms does not change this substantially.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But images that one would normally consider complex tend to have features that cannot be recognized except at significantly lower levels of compression.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Irreversible Data Compression” (from p. 572), p. 574. Scope: lossy transform-based image compression of simple, random and complex images

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Compression and recognition experiments are feasible with existing images and codecs. The broad claims about normal complexity and recognizability depend on chosen observers, features, and algorithms, limiting generalization.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Apply fixed transform codecs over a range of bit rates to preregistered simple, random, and complex images, then collect blinded human feature-recognition scores before and after coefficient reordering. The predicted class-specific rate thresholds and reordering invariance would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Relevant features require human judgments or task definitions.

Results vary across codecs and image classes.

Random images retain statistics but not semantic features.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.68
data existence: 0.85
analysis feasibility: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.6
discriminating power: 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The compression procedure itself is standard and the source images can be regenerated, so the computational half can be rerun now. Whether features remain recognizable is a perceptual variable, and public data do not already contain judgments on this exact image partition. Reordering coefficients can be tested computationally; the recognition criterion still needs an observer or an agreed proxy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compress simple, random, and complex images with a JPEG-style transform at a range of rates, optionally permuting the retained coefficients, and score whether the relevant features remain recognizable. Survival of simple and random images at rates where complex images become unrecognizable would support the claim; equal recognition thresholds would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Recognizable' is a human judgment; an error metric is only a proxy.

Quantization tables and the choice of basis change which features survive.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.56
analysis feasibility: 0.66
data existence: 0.72
operationalizability: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.55
